artifacts.delta_brief: Change: 2025 risk narrative broadens export-control risk from a China-specific licensing constraint and a modest Data Center revenue exposure to a worldwide control regime that can bar exports across many markets and reshape service delivery economics. (2024 para 81, 2024 para 82, 2025 para 122) It also adds a sharper execution risk around new architecture ramp quality and yield, explicitly linking low-yielding Blackwell material to near-term gross margin pressure. (2025 para 43) Drivers: Nvidia frames the control environment as volatile and widening, with the January 2025 AI Diffusion IFR described as limiting access to IT services markets via UVEU gating, which can push customers toward alternatives. (2025 para 137, 2025 para 122) Parallel to geopolitics, its AI market position is portrayed as pulling in competition regulators globally, creating investigative burden and potential constraints on supply allocation and foundation model partnerships. (2025 para 111) On the operational side, long lead times and demand forecasting errors remain a root cause for mismatches that have historically produced both shortages and excess inventory, setting the stage for higher stakes when product complexity rises. (2024 para 20) Caveat: The 2024 filing already flagged an inability to obtain USG licenses for restricted shipments to China and only early alternative products in small volumes, so part of the 2025 expansion may be elaboration rather than a brand new risk vector. (2024 para 81) Focuspack is a subset; additional 2024-2025 changes may sit outside these excerpts. (2025 para 111)

evidence.snippet: This mismatch has resulted in both product shortages and excess inventory, has varied across our market platforms, and has significantly harmed our financial results.
evidence.why: Baseline operational risk framing: demand forecasting errors can create shortage-or-inventory whiplash that has already harmed results, providing a comparator for 2025's expanded execution and supply-chain emphasis.

evidence.snippet: Although we have not received licenses from the USG to ship restricted products to China, we have started to ship alternatives to the China market in small volumes.
evidence.why: Shows the 2024 export-controls exposure was framed primarily as a China licensing constraint with limited alternative product shipments, a narrower aperture than the 2025 worldwide control regime.

evidence.snippet: China represented a mid-single digit percentage of our Data Center revenue in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2024 due to USG licensing requirements and we expect China to be in a similar range in the first quarter of fiscal year 2025.
evidence.why: Quantifies China revenue exposure as mid-single digit share of Data Center revenue due to licensing requirements, anchoring the 2024 magnitude before 2025 broadens the geography and mechanisms of constraint.

evidence.snippet: For example, our gross margins in the second quarter of fiscal year 2025 were negatively impacted by inventory provisions for low-yielding Blackwell material.
evidence.why: Introduces a concrete new-architecture ramp risk by tying low yields on Blackwell material to realized gross margin impact, making execution/yield a first-order financial risk in 2025.

evidence.snippet: We have also received, and continue to receive, broad requests for information from competition regulators in the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, China, and South Korea regarding our sales of GPUs and other NVIDIA products, our efforts to allocate supply, foundation models and our investments, partnerships and other
evidence.why: Adds a distinct regulatory burden narrative: global competition regulators are actively requesting information about GPUs, supply allocation, and foundation-model-related partnerships, expanding beyond generic compliance risk.

evidence.snippet: Such controls have been and may again be very broad in scope and application, prohibit us from exporting our products to any or all customers in one or more markets, including but not limited to China and over 150 countries designated “Tier 2” by the January 2025 AI Diffusion IFR, and could negatively impact our manufacturing, testing and
evidence.why: Recasts export controls as broad and potentially worldwide in effect, explicitly referencing the January 2025 AI Diffusion IFR and Tier 2 designations that could block exports across many markets and disrupt operations.

evidence.snippet: The AI Diffusion IFR would limit access to the market for IT services and computing infrastructure, by favoring a select number of government-approved firms that achieve UVEU status.
evidence.why: Clarifies the mechanism of the AI Diffusion IFR as a market-access constraint for IT services and computing infrastructure via UVEU status, implying second-order demand shifts and channel reconfiguration.

Some 2025 deltas may primarily reflect new external regulatory events (for example, export-control rule changes) rather than internally driven risk re-prioritization.
